name: Zane Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the van by half seven, a white Transit I lease through the parcel app, and I do about 140 drops across the east side until four. Then I swap to my scooter and do takeaway on the food app until nine or ten, mostly burgers and noodles to flats near the stadium. I've done it six years now, so I know which buzzers are broken and which dogs bite.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being on my own and nobody standing over me with a clipboard. What wears me out is the app changing the pay per drop without telling anyone, and the rating system that can cut you off for one bad week. My partner Lina is a nurse on nights, so half the week we just pass each other in the hallway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the hype merchants got it wrong and we can get back to arguing about the real problem, which is how the apps treat us. I'd post it in the couriers' group chat with a laughing face. Then I'd say the fight was never about robots, it was about pay per drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays the same, which is mostly fine. I earn more than most drivers I know because I do both apps and I don't take days off. The bit that bugs me is the app still cutting the rate a few pennies at a time, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my route and keep paying into the union branch, which is twelve a month. I'd keep putting six hundred a month into savings, like I do now. I wouldn't touch any of the new features the app pushes, I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed, if I'm honest. There's an itch, because the rate cuts don't stop just because the robots didn't show up. But I've got money saved and plenty of firms hiring drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the rate cuts. How much have they actually taken from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring the parcel app went from one forty a drop to one thirty-two, and nobody voted on that. Over a year that's a couple of thousand gone, give or take. I only noticed because a guy at the depot, Kofi, keeps a spreadsheet of every change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, where do you see yourself at thirty-five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably still driving, maybe for a proper firm with a contract and sick pay instead of the apps. Lina keeps saying I should get my HGV licence, the one for big lorries, and maybe I will one day. I don't like jumping, but I'd jump for sick pay.

say: I'd tell the group chat the **hype** was wrong and the real fight is still pay.
I'd say the problem was never robots, it's the **pay per drop**.
think: My life stays **the same**, and that's mostly fine because I earn well across two apps.
What bugs me is the app still **cutting the rate** a few pennies at a time.
do: Keep paying **twelve a month** to the couriers' union branch.
Keep saving **six hundred** a month, the same as now.
Ignore the app's **new features**, like I always do.
feel: Mostly **relaxed**, with money saved and plenty of driving jobs around.
A small **itch** that the rate cuts carry on regardless.
S0.quote: The fight was never about robots, it was about pay per drop.
fieldNote: He treats AI as a **distraction** from his real grievance, the apps' pay rates.
His **savings** and two-app income give him a cushion he clearly knows about.
He'd only leave the apps for **sick pay**, not for more money.

steps.text: Keep both app shifts and the union branch subscription
Put six hundred a month into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the union at the table now, not later. If the apps get smarter at planning routes, they'll use it to squeeze us, not to help us. I'd share stuff about the little pavement robots they're testing in the city centre and say watch this space.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my van work is fine for a good while, because a robot can't carry a fridge up four flights. The takeaway side worries me more, those short hops near the stadium are exactly what a pavement robot could do. If that goes, I lose maybe a third of my money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every branch meeting and push for a rule that apps can't swap us for robots without notice. I'd drop the late takeaway shifts before they drop me, and pick up more van hours. I'd still not use the AI stuff, I just don't trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit sour, to be honest. It's like watching a slow leak in a tyre you can't reach. I'm not scared yet, but I'm watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your mind about learning the AI tools if the app made them part of the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made it part of the job, I'd do the minimum, like I did with the scanner gun. I'm not against it because I'm old-fashioned. Every tool the apps have given us has been used to time our toilet breaks. That's the honest reason I won't touch AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lina say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lina would tell me to stop moaning and book the HGV course. Her ward got a scheduling system last year and she says it's fine, it just moved the stress around. She's more relaxed about this stuff than me.

say: I'd say the **union** has to be at the table now, before the apps use AI to squeeze us.
I'd share posts about the **pavement robots** being tested downtown.
think: My **van work** is safe for years because a robot can't carry a fridge upstairs.
The **takeaway** hops could go to pavement robots, about a third of my money.
do: Push at **branch meetings** for a rule on notice before robots replace drivers.
Drop late **takeaway shifts** and pick up more van hours.
Use the AI tools only at the **minimum** if forced.
feel: **Sour**, like watching a slow leak in a tyre.
S1.quote: Every tool the apps have given us has been used to time our toilet breaks. That's the honest reason I won't touch AI.
fieldNote: His refusal of AI is about **distrust of the platforms**, not fear of technology.
He clearly splits his income into **safe van work** and exposed takeaway work.
His partner is **more relaxed** about tech than he is.

steps.text: Push the union branch for notice rules on robot delivery
Swap late takeaway shifts for extra parcel van hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment governments either protect working people or they don't. I'd be at every protest, and I'd post that if robots take the deliveries, the profits have to be shared through tax. I'd be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I've got about five years before the van goes too, because the robots come a few years after the thinking stuff. The thinking stuff doesn't touch me much, I don't plan routes, the app does. But by 2031, it's different. A robot that can carry a fridge up four flights is a robot that takes my whole job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep driving and save every penny, maybe a thousand a month by dropping the gym and eating at home. I'd finally book the HGV course, not because lorries are safe but because it buys a few more years. And I'd join whatever campaign is pushing for a robot tax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a wall coming at me, slowly but for sure. I'm good with money, so I won't starve. But I'm twenty-seven and I don't know what I'd be in my thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd book the HGV course. Isn't that a hands-on job robots take too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it is, that's the joke. But lorries on motorways are a big legal fight, and the law moves slowly. I'd rather be in a job where the union is strong and the law is slow, that's my bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lina change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about buying a flat in the next two years with my savings and her overtime. I think we'd hold off, because I don't want a mortgage on a job with five years left. Lina's job is safer than mine, a robot isn't putting in a cannula any time soon.

say: I'd say governments either **protect workers** now or they don't.
I'd post that robot delivery profits must be **shared through tax**.
think: The thinking side barely touches me, but **robots by 2031** take my whole job.
I've got about **five years** before the van goes too.
do: Save about **a thousand** a month by dropping the gym and eating at home.
Book the **HGV course** to buy a few more years of work.
Join the campaign for a **robot tax**.
feel: Like a **wall** coming slowly but surely.
**Lost** about what I'd be in my thirties.
S2.quote: A robot that can carry a fridge up four flights is a robot that takes my whole job.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** as his window, since his work is almost all hands-on.
He'd **delay buying a flat** rather than borrow against a job with five years left.
His HGV plan is a bet on **slow law** and strong unions, not on lorries being safe.

steps.text: Save a thousand a month by cancelling the gym
Book the HGV lorry licence course this year
Join street campaigns for a tax on delivery robots
Put off buying a flat with Lina for two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but I'd say we've got five years to get the rules right, so stop wasting them. I'd post the dates, 2031 and 2034, and tell people to write to their councillor. I'd be less shouty and more organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with robots around 2034, I'd be thirty-five, and that's a lot of years of good money first. I could save a proper pot by then. But I'd still be driving into the same wall, only later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the HGV licence next year, not this year, and keep stacking money. I'd help the branch run a survey of drivers so we have numbers when the fight comes. And I'd let Lina and me buy the flat, because seven years of payments is something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the fast one, but it doesn't go away. It's like knowing your contract ends in a few years. You plan, but you still think about it when you're stuck in traffic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see, in those years, to feel you'd be all right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need a law that pays me out and trains me properly if a robot takes my job, not a leaflet. Something with money in it. Without that, I'm just hoping, and I don't like hoping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the depot you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, definitely. He's forty-five, he sends money home to his mum every month, and he doesn't drive anything else. I'd worry about him more than me.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to get the rules right, so stop wasting them.
I'd tell people to write to their **councillor**, with the dates.
think: Robots around 2034 give me **seven years** of good money first.
I'm still driving into **the same wall**, just later.
do: Do the **HGV licence** next year and keep saving.
Help the branch run a **driver survey** for the coming fight.
Go ahead with **buying the flat** with Lina.
feel: **Calmer** than the fast one, but it never leaves.
Like knowing a **contract ends** in a few years.
S3.quote: I need a law that pays me out and trains me properly if a robot takes my job, not a leaflet.
fieldNote: Extra time turns him from **protester to organiser**.
He'd still buy the flat, trusting **seven years** of earnings.
He worries more about an **older colleague** than about himself.

steps.text: Take the HGV licence course next year
Help run a union survey of delivery drivers
Keep saving six hundred a month toward the flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to plan, so there's no excuse for leaving drivers behind. I'd still back the union and the robot tax idea. But I wouldn't be posting about it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years plus three for the robots puts me near forty. That's long enough that I'd probably have changed jobs anyway. It still ends the same, though, and I don't trust the apps to be fair about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am for now, both apps, and keep the savings going. In a couple of years I'd look at something hands-on but harder to copy, like installing heat pumps, which a guy from my school does. I'd want the union pushing for paid retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with a cloud way off. I'm not good at planning ten years out, nobody I know is. It's a later problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't like change. Would you really leave driving for heat pumps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not unless I had to. Knowing me, I'd talk about leaving driving for years and then do it at the last minute. My partner Lina would laugh at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the union to win in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid retraining with a wage while you learn, not evening classes after a ten-hour shift. And a say in how fast the apps bring in robots. That's it, those two things.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to plan, so no excuse to leave drivers behind.
I'd still back the **union** and the robot tax, just less loudly.
think: Robots around 2039 put me **near forty**, when I might have moved on anyway.
It ends **the same**, and I don't trust the apps to be fair.
do: Carry on with **both apps** and keep the savings going.
Look at **heat pump installing** in a couple of years.
Back the union's push for **paid retraining**.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with a cloud far off.
Admits it's a **later problem** in his head.
S4.quote: I'd talk about leaving driving for years and then do it at the last minute. My partner Lina would laugh at that.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him **postpone** the decision, which suits his resistance to change.
He wants two concrete wins: **paid retraining** and a say on robot pace.
He's honest that he'd move **at the last minute**.

steps.text: Keep working both delivery apps as now
Ask a school friend about heat pump installer training
Back the union campaign for retraining with a wage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because I'd have the least time and the apps would have all the power. What would help is a law that pays drivers out and trains them on a wage. Money, not leaflets.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I blame. I blame the app companies more than the robots. Robots are just the next tool in the same hands. The apps have already shown how they treat us.

headlineQuote: I blame the app companies more than the robots. Robots are just the next tool in the same hands.
portrait: Zane is 27, drives a **parcel van** by day and a **takeaway scooter** by night, earning well across two apps.
He has strong **savings**, a partner who's a nurse, and plenty of driving jobs nearby.
He's a **union** man who distrusts the apps and refuses AI tools as their weapon.
He's calm about the plateau but **alarmed** when robots arrive by 2031, his whole job being hands-on.
With more warning he **postpones** change, planning an HGV licence and maybe heat pumps.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's the least time and the apps hold all the power.
whatWouldHelp: A law that **pays drivers out** and trains them on a wage, not leaflets.
